thread.title: Charlotte developer asks: Was submitting multiple sites a mistake in quest for Amazon's HQ2?

author: Ashley Fahey
title: Charlotte developer asks: Was submitting multiple sites a mistake in quest for Amazon's HQ2?
text: Jan 18, 2018, 11:59am EST Updated Jan 18, 2018, 1:47pm EST No $5 billion investment. No addition of 50,000 jobs. And no #Prime mover and shaker to bring endless publicity as well as a mini-economic boom. Charlotte and its outlying counties whiffed on all of that and more on Thursday, when Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ: AMZN) scratched the area from its list of potential sites for the HQ2 campus touted by the online retailer for months. Rod Crider , CEO of the Salisbury-Rowan County Economic Development Commission, said the Charlotte region gained valuable experience by making a serious run at HQ2. And he emphasized the importance of using those new insights to pursue other companies in the months ahead. "Our region learned some valuable lessons during the process that will strengthen our competitiveness for other projects in the future," Crider said, touting a local effort that "put together an amazing bid that captured the promise and energy of the region." Twenty cities made Amazon's shortlist for its second headquarters. Several of Charlotte's peer cities in the Southeast did end up among the finalists, including Atlanta, Raleigh and Nashville, Tenn. A total of 238 cities across North America initially pursued HQ2. Economic development executives and analysts acknowledged disappointment that neither Charlotte nor Hickory, another N.C. bidder, are among the finalists. Catawba County Economic Development Corp. submitted a separate bid for HQ2, offering a site located in southern Catawba County. "We were always realistic and our secondary objective was to expose leaders to the 1,000-plus acre site we had proposed, which was accomplished," said Scott Millar, Catawba EDC president. "We also generated national exposure in The Wall Street Journal , MSNBC and many others, which was another objective." Charlotte submitted a bid with more than 20 potential sites in multiple counties. Ballantyne was one of the sites submitted to Amazon though the Charlotte Regional Partnership in the local effort. "In the economic development business, you understand you will lose more than you win," said Ned Curran , president of Ballantyne owner Northwood Office. "We are all better for the effort, and we will continue to focus on the significant number of other opportunities that are out there. In the meantime, we should all wish Raleigh well in its pursuit of HQ2." Best approach? Those sentiments were shared among other developers in the Charlotte region, several of whom submitted their own sites to be considered in Charlotte's bid. “I’m glad somewhere in North Carolina is on the list,” real estate developer Johnny Harris told the Charlotte Business Journal . His company, Lincoln Harris , is working with Crescent Communities on a substantial mixed-use project in southwest Charlotte called the River District , another site considered to be a potential home for HQ2 if Amazon had selected the city. “I’m not surprised by anything in a process like this," Harris said. With Raleigh still in the running, Harris said a potential benefit would be for the Triangle to invest in a light-rail system connecting Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill. “I hope they have the guts to build light rail, something they should have done 20 years ago — it would help the whole state.” Brian Leary , president of commercial and mixed use at Crescent Communities, expressed similar sentiments. He said he was disappointed, but not surprised, that Charlotte was left off the list. "Sending 22 different options, spreading it thin across the board, I’m not so sure that was a really strong approach," he said. He added, though, that he doesn't know much about the local bid and whether that might have impacted Charlotte's chances. He said many of the cities that made the list "shouldn't have anything on us." Mac Holladay , CEO of Market Street Services, an Atlanta firm that consults with communities on economic development and other strategies, disagreed. "I don't know that submitting multiple sites hurt Charlotte," he said. Communities in Georgia submitted their own proposals without consulting with the state, he added. Atlanta was the only Georgia city to survive the winnowing process, though. Looking forward Some local leaders are already calling for a reboot of recruiting pitches. Maintaining the enthusiasm generated by the possibility of landing Amazon should be balanced with a thorough analysis of what worked — and what didn’t. If Charlotte can build a reputation for attracting creative class workers and companies as, for example, Austin and Nashville have, it might have a better chance at landing projects akin to Amazon HQ2 in the future, Leary said. Republican councilman Tariq Bokhari pointed to the disclosure this week by Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL) that it is planning another campus of its own, which could house as many as 20,000 employees. “This is not a case of doing a find-replace and putting in Apple instead of Amazon,” Bokhari said, referring to the HQ2 bid simple being reshaped to lure Apple. “We need to take what we did with Amazon and take it to the next level.” Bokhari confessed to being “flabbergasted” by Charlotte’s absence from the 20 HQ2 finalist cities named by Amazon on Thursday. He pointed to Charlotte Douglas International Airport, the presence of Bank of America’s headquarters and Wells Fargo’s East Coast hub, population growth and other factors as ones that would warrant serious consideration. And, while he is happy Raleigh was included, Bokhari said the capital city’s presence erases any possibility that Charlotte may have been affected by controversy over House Bill 2 since it was a state-wide law. HB2, widely blamed for costing the state multiple corporate expansions and major events, was partially repealed in March 2017. Among the takeaways, he said, are a need to closely scrutinize and review how the city and region approach recruiting pitches. Beyond that, Bokhari hopes Amazon — which has benefited from attendant publicity throughout the HQ2 campaign while also receiving “a treasure chest of consumer and demographic data” — will lend bid cities insight on what worked and didn’t with their bids and what their strengths and weaknesses are. “I hope (Amazon) will give back to make us all better,” Bokhari said. Charlotte should use this as an opportunity to "look in the mirror" at how the city approaches and competes to win economic development projects, Leary said, adding that that extends to approach to government, infrastructure needs and incubating and driving the tech economy. "How are we positioning ourselves to be competitive day in and day out?" Leary said. "It’s not just when we’re chasing the big whale. Companies are following talent and people. If we can win hearts and minds of talented people and their friends, and this is a place where people want to go ... we are going to win things like this future." Business Pulse
